item.title: When "I’m Sorry" Isn’t Enough
item.description:
Forgiveness

When "I’m Sorry" Isn’t Enough

What do we really want when we ask for an apology?

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • Genuine apologies are about more than saying "I'm sorry."
  • There's often a gap in understanding between the person who caused the harm and the person who experienced it.
  • Acknowledgment and validation are the starting points for reconciliation.
Source: kalhh / Pixabay

“You owe me an apology!”

Have you ever found yourself saying this to someone who has hurt or disappointed you? Maybe they forgot a lunch date or dropped the ball on a favour they promised to do.

You want an apology, but why? Will hearing “I am sorry” actually help? It can’t undo the damage, un-miss the lunch, or retroactively make things right. So why do those three words hold so much power?

Research suggests that what we want most may not be an expression of regret at all. We want the other person to acknowledge what they did and show us that they understand why it matters to us.

Apologies aren’t about rewriting history. They can’t erase the harmful act or undo what happened. In fact, a good apology does the opposite: It confirms what happened. Rather than glossing over the wrongdoing, the person who caused the harm actually acknowledges it. They say, “I’m sorry I missed our lunch. It was inconsiderate of me to keep you waiting,” rather than offering a simple “Oops, sorry!”

But why does that acknowledgment matter so much?

The Magnitude Gap

We generally don’t expect to be treated badly by others, so when it happens, it can be jarring. Imagine that a friend cancels plans at the last minute. You may interpret their behaviour as inconsiderate, as if they don’t value you or your time. You might even question your own perceptions, wondering whether it was your fault or whether you did something to deserve that kind of treatment.

Now imagine that your friend responds with a simple “sorry!” and immediately moves on. The original offence is no longer the only issue. Now you may also feel that your friend doesn’t understand, or maybe doesn’t care, why you’re upset.

This disconnect is what social psychologist Roy Baumeister (1997) has described as the “magnitude gap.” It refers to the fact that there’s often a discrepancy in how victims and perpetrators interpret transgressions: Victims generally view a wrongdoing as more significant, impactful, and long-lasting than the person who caused it does.

This gap can be the reason why some apologies don’t land effectively. The person who was hurt wants acknowledgement, clarity, and reassurance that they didn’t deserve the poor treatment. The person who caused the harm may be more concerned with avoiding blame, anger, or liability.

In order to mend the relationship, a good apology needs to close the magnitude gap. And, as it turns out, the words “I’m sorry” may be the least important part of the equation.

What We Really Want From an Apology

My colleagues and I conducted a series of experiments to explore how validation, or the feeling that another person recognizes and understands our experience, can influence forgiveness (Eaton et al., 2006).

We created an online game in which participants competed in a game against an adversary who treated them unfairly, causing them to lose. Afterward, the adversary offered one of four messages: a simple apology (“I’m sorry”), fact-based validation (“I treated you unfairly”), both an apology and validation, or neither an apology nor validation.

We then measured how validated participants felt and how willing they were to forgive their adversary.

As we expected, when the adversary said nothing, participants reported low validation and low forgiveness. But simply hearing “I’m sorry” didn’t help much either.

The best outcome was when the adversary acknowledged the wrongdoing. Participants felt more validated, and this feeling of validation was associated with greater forgiveness. Remarkably, in our experiment, it didn’t seem to matter whether the adversary said “I’m sorry” or not; validation alone was just as effective as validation paired with “I’m sorry.”

Why? Because acknowledgment creates a feeling of shared reality, an understanding that both parties are on the same page about what happened. That’s why apologies like “I’m sorry you’re mad” or “I’m sorry if I hurt you” don’t tend to work very well. They don’t indicate that the offender truly understands why the victim is upset. And it’s this validation that is most likely to lead to forgiveness.

The Missing Ingredient

When we want an apology, we aren’t necessarily looking for an elaborate expression of remorse, but just the words “I’m sorry” are usually not sufficient either. We’re looking for the person who hurt us to acknowledge what they did and take responsibility for it. Research on apologies shows that taking responsibility is one of the single most critical components of an effective apology (Lewicki et al., 2016).

Taking responsibility can help close the magnitude gap. By acknowledging the wrongdoing and its impact, the person who caused the harm shows that they recognize the other person’s experience. This helps bridge the distance between the harm doer’s need for self-protection and the hurt person’s need for validation. And that’s when real repair begins.

This doesn’t mean that validating someone’s experience requires agreeing with everything they say. The people involved can disagree about the details while still acknowledging that the action was hurtful or inconsiderate.

Acknowledgement isn’t a magic fix, but it’s a starting point. Genuine remorse, restitution, and evidence of changed behaviour may be needed before trust can be fully restored, especially when the harm is serious. But until the person who caused the harm shows that they understand why their actions were hurtful, reconciliation is unlikely. These are some of the issues I explore in my upcoming book, Say It Like You Mean It: The Science of Apologies and How They Might Just Save Us.

The next time you find yourself wanting an apology, consider what it is you’re really hoping to hear. Is it simply “I’m sorry,” or do you want something more: validation that the other person acknowledges what happened, understands why it matters, and accepts responsibility for their actions?

And if you’re the person who needs to apologize, try starting there. Before explaining your intentions or defending your actions, show the other person that you understand their experience.

You don’t just owe them an apology. You owe them validation.

item.title: Why Everything Your Partner Says Irritates You
item.description:
Relationships

Why Everything Your Partner Says Irritates You

Use these three steps to soften negative sentiment override.

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • In a tense relationship, partners read each other negatively even when the message is neutral or kind.
  • Disconnection starts when one person's love tank is empty and they get more complaints than warmth.
  • The gap between one's negative read and what the other actually owns is what hurts the relationship.
Source: Assael Romanelli

Co-authored by Galit Romanelli

Jasmine rolls her eyes. Joel is still talking.

He hasn't filed the taxes. He tried five times and never succeeded. When she asks him to pick something up at the supermarket, he forgets what she asked for. As we work, Joel defends himself with every sentence. The longer he goes, the more childish he looks.

They are stuck in the mommy-son dance, and it is a dance we've seen a million times in the clinic.

The toll Jasmine pays is that every time she opens her mouth, she is interpreted as an upset, tired, disappointed mommy testing him.

I stop the dialogue. "You are stuck in negative sentiment override."

"What's that?" Joel asks.

"Let me tell you a joke. How do you know a lawyer is lying?"

Jasmine jumps in, laughing. "He opens his mouth!"

The three of us laugh. The room opens up a bit.

"Exactly. And how do we know Joel is being childish and irresponsible? He opens his mouth. How do we know Jasmine is unhappy and disappointed? She opens her mouth." They smile and look at each other.

Negative Sentiment Override

Researchers John and Julie Gottman found that partners in a tense relationship start to interpret each other's actions and intentions negatively, even when they are neutral or positive. They call it negative sentiment override (NSO).

It starts when your love tank is empty, and you get more complaints than warmth. Disappointment and insult color your relational glasses. After that, anything they say, whether it's "what's wrong?" or "I love you," gets read in that unfavorable light.

We see NSO as an innate defense mechanism that protects us when we don't feel safe. That is why it is so hard to soften. And it is usually mutual. Every interpretation Joel gives to Jasmine's behavior strengthens the one she gives to his.

The Gottmans named it and gave initial instructions. In the clinic we built a practical approach.

1. Map the Loop

Both partners need to see the systemic pattern of mutual interpretations.

I ask Jasmine for her default interpretation of Joel: "He's inefficient, because he's deficient." What does that make you feel? "Angry and disconnected." And then how do you usually react? She names three. She disengages and does it herself. She gives an "unsuccessful motivational speech." Or she throws a jab dressed as a question.

Joel's default interpretation of Jasmine: "She's testing me, and she's already disappointed." That makes him feel trapped and helpless. Then he lashes out to feel less bad. Or he does the task on a kamikaze mission, knowing it won't make "mommy" happy. Or he explains himself in detail, which is defending himself.

Map the actions, not only the interpretations. The drawing shows couples how fast their brains lock the dance, and how they both feed it.

Source: Romanelli

2. Compare the Numbers and Own Your Shadow

Then I ask each for a percentage. "Out of 100 percent of the times your partner communicates with you, how often do you have that negative interpretation?" Jasmine said 80 percent. Joel said 90.

Second question, which puts that read next to the negativity actually intended. "What percentage of the time are you really in that mode?" Joel owned 50. Jasmine owned 80.

They both overshoot. Jasmine's read of Joel runs 30 points hot. Not because he's inefficient and deficient, but because he's different. Joel's read of Jasmine runs 10 points hot. She is not looking for a son to manage. She is looking for a partner. Seeing the size of your own false positive is what makes you curious again.

The numbers only work if you own your shadow. We all behave nastily to our partner sometimes. Schnarch calls it normal marital sadism. NSO develops because partners deny or minimize their unavoidable aggression, which leaves their partner mind-reading.

So own it every time you behave badly, even retroactively. "Yesterday, when I rolled my eyes at you, I really did judge you about dinner. Sorry." That is how your partner's somatic polygraph, the poly-body, learns the difference between their interpretation and you actually being nasty.

Source: Romanelli

3. Pick a Code Word

Play is the lubricant of relationships. One playful technique is code words, which keep partners collaborative when one of them is flooding. If you can remember the code word, you have enough prefrontal cortex left to not go into your usual violin.

Each partner picks one. Nothing triggering or dramatic. A short, playful word with a positive association.

Joel chooses "Kinder" to replace this sentence: "Jasmine, everything you're saying is landing on me as if you're the disappointed mommy, and I don't want to go into feeling trapped and helpless."

Jasmine chooses "Bueno" for this one: "Joel, right now I'm interpreting everything you say as an immature child, so I'm checking with you. Are you in child mode?"

When you're flooded, or around guests, these sentences are hard to remember or express. Saying bueno is easy.

When your partner uses the word, stop, breathe, and survey your poly-body. If you're behaving negatively, own it and take a timeout. If their interpretation is wrong, say so calmly and hold on to yourself. Then they'll have to choose to believe you and soften the interpretation. If they can't, they ask for the timeout.

Source: Romanelli

Clean Your Glasses

It may not be just your interpretation. Maybe Joel is actually inefficient and deficient. Maybe Jasmine has lost her ability to see him with love. I don't know.

What we focus on is helping both partners clean their ears and eyes, so they can correctly assess their current marriage, before negotiating the next marriage they want.

Oftentimes the biggest enemy for couples is not each other. It is their filters, full of calcified negativity, preventing them from meeting in the truth. Cleaning the glasses turns relational exclamation marks into question marks.

Galit Romanelli is a relationship coach, Ph.D. candidate, and co-creator of The Remarriage Roadmap.

item.title: Winning Negotiation Strategy: The Power of the Pause
item.description:
Persuasion

Winning Negotiation Strategy: The Power of the Pause

Turn-taking in business communication builds credibility and chemistry.

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • Dynamic turn-taking conversation builds relationships.
  • Long pauses usually prompt negative impressions of communicators.
  • Brief pauses encourage listeners to acknowledge what is said, creating a positive impression of communicators.
Source: Erwin Bosman / Pixabay

In business, much is accomplished not on paper, but in person. That includes the dynamics of discussion—both speaking and listening. The way you speak and take turns speaking has more of an impact than people realize. Research explains.

Negotiating Turn-taking

Matteo Di Stasi et al. (2024) investigated what type of discussion dynamics impacted objective and relational outcomes in bargaining. Studying 239 online negotiation recordings, they examined interconnected factors such as speech rate, speaking time, interruptions, pauses, and response time. They found that several of the measures they examined uniquely predict outcomes in videoconference negotiations, both objectively and relationally.

On the objective level, Di Stasi et al. found that negotiators who speak more and faster, and with fewer pauses, were able to achieve better deals. Yet at the relational level, they found that negotiators who did not interrupt and engaged in more dynamic turn length were better liked. Because both outcomes can produce positive results, they note that taken together, they indicate that good deals are made in part through conversation dynamics.

The Relational Power of the Pause

More recent research has examined the power of the pause in goal-oriented collaboration. Alex B. Van Zant et al. (2025) studied the impact of pausing in collaborative conversations—defined as “cooperative, task-oriented dialogues” where two or more people collaborate in pursuit of a common goal. They began by acknowledging generally that long pauses usually prompt negative impressions of communicators, while short pauses elicit assents—such as “uh-huh” or “yeah” or “uh-huh"—in collaborative conversation. Because assents create positive perceptions of speakers, pausing during collaborative conversations makes communicators appear more helpful.

Yet pauses have their place within the larger context of conversation. Van Zant et al. note that collaborative conversations constitute a dynamic exchange including listening and providing verbal feedback to signal to speakers their words are understood as intended. Allowing conversation partners to provide backchannel responses—interjecting understanding while speakers talk—allows conversation partners to provide positive feedback without taking over the conversation, prompting collaboration in furtherance of achieving a shared mutual understanding. Van Zant et al. note that while backchannel responses can include affective reactions such as “Wow!”, assenting is most common.

Van Zant et al. note this approach is in contrast to competitive dialogue, which involves a communicator attempting to dominate the conversation to impose their personal viewpoint. Collaborative dialogue, in contrast, involves listeners actively seeking to comprehend the assumptions, knowledge, and perspectives of conversation partners. Backchannel responses are therefore far more common in conversations that are collaborative rather than competitive.

Pause Wisely

When it comes to pauses, however, there can apparently be too much of a good thing. Long silences can undermine social connection and reduce credibility. Van Zant et al. note that although speakers are wise to think carefully before speaking, long response delays of 3 seconds or longer not only disrupt conversational flow and satisfaction, but they also portray speakers as less competent.

As a result of their research, Van Zant et al. demonstrated that brief pauses while speaking are a strategic, practical method of increasing active listening from conversation partners. Although their research is useful for organizations, employees, and collaborative communicators, pausing during such conversations can encourage assent and increase their perceived helpfulness.

So, whether helping a customer or attempting to impress a colleague, pausing can help create a more positive image and create better outcomes personally and professionally.

item.title: "Why Did They Do That?"
item.description:
Locus of Control

"Why Did They Do That?"

Why "why" questions can keep you stuck.

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • "Why" questions fuel rumination.
  • Insight doesn't require acceptance.
  • Choice restores agency.

Have you ever spent hours trying to figure out why someone did something that hurt you? Whether it's a family member, partner, or co-worker, it's easy to spiral around endless “why” questions.

“Why would they say that?”

“Why would they do that?”

“Why didn't they respond to me?”

"Why are they being so annoying?"

When someone hurts us, our brains want an explanation. We assume that if we can understand the reason behind someone's behavior, we'll feel better about what happened. As a psychotherapist, I've spent my whole career trying to understand why people do what they do. Understanding behavior can be useful. But there's a point when asking "why" stops producing insight and starts producing a downward spiral of rumination.

Rumination is a pattern of repetitive thinking about distressing experiences and their possible causes and consequences. Research by Nolen-Hoeksema and colleagues (2008) found that rumination can intensify negative emotions, interfere with problem-solving, and contribute to depression and anxiety. You might spend three hours analyzing someone's childhood, attachment style, personality, and possible motivations. You might even arrive at a compelling explanation.

But then what?

The Insight Trap

Understanding why someone did something doesn't mean you have to tolerate their behavior. Explanation is not a synonym for excuse, but the two can get conflated. Someone can have perfectly understandable reasons for behaving in ways you find unacceptable. But when we're focused on understanding someone else's internal world, we can lose sight of our own experience.

Research on repetitive negative thinking suggests that getting caught in analysis can maintain emotional distress, while more concrete forms of processing may support effective problem-solving (Watkins, 2008). In other words, analyzing a situation and responding to it are two different activities. You can spend an enormous amount of energy attempting to understand someone's motivations without making a single decision about what you want to do next.

External Locus of Control: When Someone Else Holds the Answers

Psychologist Julian Rotter (1966) introduced the concept of locus of control, which refers to whether people believe the outcomes in their lives are primarily influenced by their own actions or by external forces. People with a more external locus of control tend to attribute outcomes to circumstances, luck, or other people, while those with a more internal locus of control tend to believe their own actions can influence outcomes.

When we become consumed with understanding why someone behaved a certain way, we can inadvertently place our ability to move forward in someone else's hands. We convince ourselves that we need an explanation, an apology, or some kind of acknowledgment before we can decide what to do. Our attention becomes focused on something outside our control: another person's thoughts, feelings, and motivations.

An internal locus of control recognizes the influence we have over our own actions and decisions. We can't control whether someone tells the truth, offers an apology, or changes their behavior. But we can decide what we're willing to accept, what conversations we want to have, and what steps we're prepared to take. We can acknowledge that someone hurt us without needing to solve the mystery of why.

Three Steps to Get Unstuck from Rumination

Here's a simple shift that can save you hours of spiraling.

Step 1: Name It

Instead of asking, "Why did they do that?" try saying, "I don't like that they did that."

Step 2: Own It

Once you recognize you do not like a behavior, ask yourself, "What are my choices?"

Step 3: Do a Micro Yes

Once you identify your choices, take one step in the direction of one of those choices, no matter how small. The most microscopic step forward is preferable to none.

Here's why this works.

Asking "why" disconnects us from our autonomy and choice power. Saying "I don't like that they did that" brings our attention back to our own experience. Then, asking "What are my choices?" shifts our focus toward decisions and actions within our influence.

You might decide to have a conversation, establish a boundary, change your expectations, or reconsider the relationship. You might decide that the behavior isn't worth addressing. You are empowered to make decisions regardless of whether you ever receive a satisfying explanation. You can understand someone's behavior and still dislike it. You can empathize with someone's circumstances and still refuse to accept bad behavior.

You may never get a satisfying answer to why someone did what they did. But you still get to decide what you do next.

item.title: Let's Talk About Menopause
item.description:
Menopause

Let's Talk About Menopause

More than a hormonal transition, menopause is a psychological shift as well.

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • Stigma around menopause has created a lack of awareness and accurate information.
  • Menopause has been gaining more recognition as a biopsychosocial transition that affects the whole person.
  • Menopause affects not only reproductive health but cardiovascular health, sleep, cognition, and mental health.

Menopause is often discussed in terms of hot flashes, night sweats, and changing hormone levels. Yet for many women, menopause represents something far more profound: a biopsychosocial transition that touches nearly every aspect of life, including emotional well-being, relationships, cognition, work, and identity.

While fluctuating estrogen and progesterone levels can contribute to mood changes, anxiety, sleep disruption, and difficulties with concentration, menopause rarely occurs in isolation. Midlife often coincides with major life transitions such as caring for aging parents, navigating career changes, reassessing long-term relationships, experiencing children leaving home, and confronting questions about aging, purpose, and mortality.

As psychologists, we know that biological changes unfold within a broader psychological and social context. Menopause is no exception.

Recent reports from the 2025 American Psychological Association Presidential Task Force on Women's Health and Well-Being During Midlife and Menopause emphasize that menopause is not simply a medical event but a significant biopsychosocial experience that warrants greater attention from researchers, health care professionals, clinicians, policymakers, and medical and mental health systems. The task force's reports highlight persistent research gaps in understanding women's mental health during midlife while also calling for more comprehensive, evidence-informed, culturally responsive, and trauma-informed models of care (APA, 2026).

The reports underscore several important realities. Midlife and menopause affect roughly half the population, yet many women continue to encounter misinformation, stigma, inadequate provider training, and fragmented care. The task force recommends strengthening interdisciplinary collaboration among medical and mental health professionals, expanding clinician education on menopause, improving access to quality care, and increasing research focused on the psychological dimensions of the menopause transition (APA, 2026).

One of the most important contributors to this emerging body of work is Dr. Rebecca Thurston, a leading menopause researcher and co-chair of the APA task force reports. Drawing upon decades of research, including the landmark Study of Women's Health Across the Nation (SWAN), Thurston has helped illuminate how menopause affects not only reproductive health but also cardiovascular health, sleep, cognition, brain aging, and mental health.

In a recent episode of my Wellness in Today's World podcast, Thurston discussed menopause as a whole-person experience rather than a narrow hormonal condition. She highlighted growing evidence that symptoms such as hot flashes and sleep disruption may provide important information about broader health processes, including cardiovascular and brain health. Her work encourages both women and health care professionals to think more expansively about menopause and its implications for long-term well-being.

Importantly, the conversation around menopause is evolving. Historically, menopause has often been framed primarily as a period of loss or decline. Emerging research tells a more nuanced story. While some women experience substantial distress and impairment, others report increased self-confidence, greater self-awareness, stronger boundary-setting, and a renewed sense of purpose. The APA reports (2025) explicitly recognize both the challenges and strengths associated with this life stage, emphasizing resilience, growth, and adaptation.

Psychological support can play a vital role during this transition. Effective interventions may include psychoeducation, cognitive-behavioral approaches, mindfulness-based strategies, sleep interventions, stress management techniques, and strengthening of social connections. Mental health professionals are uniquely positioned to help women differentiate between symptoms related to menopause, life stressors, and mental health conditions while supporting healthy adaptation through midlife.

Perhaps the most important message is that menopause deserves recognition as a significant developmental transition that often extends into periods before and beyond when menopause is typically experienced. It is not merely the end of reproductive capacity but a complex intersection of biological change, psychological development, and social transition.

As awareness grows and research advances, we have an opportunity to move beyond stigma and toward a more comprehensive understanding of women's health during midlife and menopause. This can only be accomplished through scientific rigor and compassionate whole-person care. Taking a biopsychosocial systems approach allows us to support flourishing, resilience, and well-being throughout the second half of life.

item.title: Youth, Love, Loneliness, and Politics
item.description:
Politics

Youth, Love, Loneliness, and Politics

Our national ethos of polarization is hardest on the young.

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • Young people are particularly susceptible to the negative effects of social and political polarization.
  • Intolerance of different perspectives and high reactivity afflict youth who think in absolutes or extremes.
  • Political beliefs are preferences that should be grounded in basic humanity and moral character.

The harmful effects of our polarized political and social climate result, in part, from the function of anxiety as a general central nervous system alarm, which makes the brain look for threats.

Young people are particularly susceptible to the negative effects of polarized thinking. Lacking sufficient life experience, they can easily mistake anxiety about a political or social policy for anxiety about love and friendship, and vice versa.

In the best of times, young people have a low tolerance of intellectual ambiguity and disagreement, which can undermine their relationships. Low tolerance of disagreement and ambiguity is normal in the developing sense of self, when feelings of certainty are more important to emotional coherence than intellectual analysis. But in turbulent times, when focused on things they can’t control, like politics and social policy, they feel powerless, which makes them irritable, intellectually rigid or superficial, and less likely to sustain close relationships.

Intolerance of different perspectives and high emotional reactivity affect many Americans in our times, but it’s especially intense in youth who tend to think in absolutes or extremes. Couched in ideology, polarized thinking, with its inherent biases and blind spots, inevitably deteriorates relationships, if not blocks them altogether. For any close relationship to succeed, we cannot have the mindset of, "I will only love you if you agree with me."

Red flag disagreements are those that devalue, dismiss, or disrespect.

Under stress, we tend to see the world through the lens of our core vulnerability—fear or shame—and make projections onto others based on them. The immature prefrontal cortex is prone to use projections as shortcut judgments. Projections make it impossible to see others as complex people, independent of our feelings about them.

Political beliefs are preferences that should be grounded in basic humanity and moral character. When they are not, disagreements seem like personal assaults, even abuse.

It’s especially hard for generations raised with social media to grasp how it amplifies stress and magnifies disagreements, and that it cannot adequately address the enormous complexity of social problems.

All the above contribute to the alarming rise in anxiety and depression among young people.

How to Escape

I believe that political and social polarization will reach a tipping point when rejecting groups of people for any reason becomes too exhausting. In the meantime, if you want to escape political narcissism, be more curious than judgmental. Look for what you can learn from different perspectives, rather than reasons to reject them. Look for what is true, even among what you regard as falsehoods. Replace polemic thinking with dialectic analysis, which synthesizes the best of all positions. Don’t settle for the superficial and heavily biased information contained in labels.

Recognize that the crucial characteristics of functional close relationships are compassion and kindness, not political or social agreement.

item.title: The Discovery of Tourette Syndrome
item.description:
Career

The Discovery of Tourette Syndrome

The life and times of Gilles de la Tourette.

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • In 1885, Gilles de la Tourette, a neurology trainee, was asked to "bring some order to the chaos of choreas."
  • The syndrome he found, including tics, echolalia, and coprolalia, was named after him by Jean-Martin Charcot.
  • Afterwards, Gilles de la Tourette devoted himself to studying hysteria, the central interest of his mentor.

Tourette syndrome, which among other symptoms can produce simple and complex tics, verbal repetitions of what others say (echolalia), and uncontrollable outbursts of obscene language (coprolalia), affects roughly 400,000 American children and adults. Though the French neurologist Gilles de la Tourette (1857-1904) is remembered today for his description of the syndrome in 1885, he would have been quite surprised, as he considered himself a lifelong researcher in hysteria. In this post, we will explore his colorful life and see how this came about.

Gilles de la Tourette, who had been born on Oct. 30, 1857, near Loudun, in the Poitou region in west-central France, went to medical school in Poitiers, and came to Paris to continue his studies in 1877. By 1881 he had become an intern, and in 1884 came to study with Jean-Martin Charcot (1825-1893), who is often described as the father of modern neurology. Charcot is credited with discovering diseases such as multiple sclerosis and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and suggesting that the "shaking palsy" be named after the English surgeon James Parkinson.

A depiction by André Brouillet (1857-1914) of Charcot giving a clinical lesson on hysteria. Gilles de la Tourette is at left wearing a white apron.
Source: André Brouillet in Wikimedia Commons/Public domain.

How Tourette Syndrome Was Identified and Named

Although Charcot’s attention was turning in those years to hysteria, he asked his trainee to clarify a particular group of patients, in his words, to "bring some order to the chaos of choreas," a term which as used then referred to a wide range of involuntary movements. Gilles de la Tourette was aware of what were known as ‘startle syndromes,’ in conditions including ‘latah’ in Malaysia, ‘myriachit’ in Siberia, as well as the 'jumping Frenchmen of Maine.' He was particularly interested in the latter, which had a familial aspect, with symptoms first appearing in childhood. In 1885 he wrote a paper describing some nine patients with similar conditions. One of the most colorful of these, the Marquise de Dampierre (1799-1884), had in fact been described in 1825 by Dr. Jean Itard in Paris. She had a certain notoriety, and was well known in high society for her frequent utterances of obscenities. At a clinical conference later in the year, Charcot announced that this maladie des tics should be named after Gilles de la Tourette. As an aside: It is said that Charcot chose his surname in part because of its melodious quality; it actually is comprised of two poetry meters going back to ancient Greece, an iambus following a dactyl (1). It seems likely, however, that neither Charcot nor his precocious trainee recognized the full significance of what they had described.

The Initial Reception of Gilles de la Tourette’s Work

The paper received little recognition at the time, and Gilles de la Tourette never wrote about it again aside from one article in 1899. Instead, he turned his attention to what had become Charcot’s main interest. In 1870, a ward which specialized in treating ‘hystero-epilepsy’ was closed due to deterioration of the building which housed it, and approximately 150 such patients had been transferred to his service. Charcot found himself responsible for a large number of patients with what was then known as hysteria, and he became very interested in their condition. It was an illness in which patients—women and also men, he was quick to point out, establishing a ward to study male hysterics—manifested a variety of striking symptoms, for which no medical cause could be found. Among these were convulsions, trance-like states, tetany, spasms, and periods of amnesia. Charcot was a charismatic figure, whose demonstrations of the dramatic behavior of patients with hysteria, whom he believed could be treated with hypnosis, drew the attention of not only the medical community, including Sigmund Freud, but also journalists as well as dancers and actresses such as Sarah Bernhardt. This was a heady atmosphere for a young neurologist finishing up his training, and Gilles de la Tourette spent most of his professional life studying it.

As the years went on, Gilles de la Tourette did study after study, reporting, for instance, that he believed one could write with a finger upon the skin of such patients (dermatographia) or that when cut, they bleed less than others. Ultimately he published a three-volume summation of his understanding of hysteria in 1881 through 1885. Though he studied many other conditions such as epilepsy and the legal aspects of hypnosis, he also engaged in public debates on social issues, and was the chief physician of the Paris World’s Fair in 1900. He undoubtedly would have considered his tomes on hysteria the epitome of his work. Today, many of his findings seem quaint, and the diagnosis of hysteria per se was appropriately removed from the major psychiatric nomenclature (the DSM) in 1980, its various components dispersed among other conditions including conversion disorder, and now more currently in "functional neurological symptom disorder" and other diagnoses (2). It’s a good reminder that the work that reflects one’s passion can easily be mistaken for the work which was most lasting across time.

Why Gilles de la Tourette Left His Eponymous Syndrome to Others

Another intriguing aspect of Gilles de la Tourette’s description of his syndrome is the way in which he moved on to other things, leaving it for others to work out the implications of what he had found. It turns out that this has happened a number of times in the history of medicine. As but one example, after discovering Penicillium mold in a culture dish of staphylococcus bacteria on Sept. 3, 1928, Alexander Fleming published his discovery in 1929, only briefly describing its possible utility as a medicine. After 1931, his interests turned elsewhere. It was only in 1938 that Howard Florey, at Oxford, saw Fleming’s article and realized its significance. He and chemist Ernst Chain developed it as a medicine, first given to a human in 1941, and within a few years it was widely used for treatment of infected wounds in World War II. A similar phenomenon occurred after the re-discovery of lithium as a treatment for bipolar disorder by John Cade in 1949 (3).

Over the decades, the understanding of Tourette syndrome has evolved, including modern treatments which began with haloperidol in the 1960s, and the view that it involves autoimmune and genetic influences, as well as the interaction of genetic predisposition with environmental factors. But it all began when a trainee was asked by his mentor to clarify a particular group of movement disorders, had a syndrome named after him in part because of his poetic name, left it to others to realize the importance of his finding, and went on to devote his career to an illness that in a sense no longer exists. Science moves forward in complex ways.

item.title: Why Some Boys Feel They Have to Hide Their Love of Reading
item.description:
Parenting

Why Some Boys Feel They Have to Hide Their Love of Reading

Many boys learn early on that there's a social price to pay for liking to read.

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • Kids often brag about not having read a book “in years” and tease the ones who have.
  • For boys who aren't particularly athletic, the social price of being smart or loving books can be high.
  • Parents can help boys who like to read by normalizing attempts to hide it and teaching about social pressure.

I grew up in the 1960s and '70s when reading was popular. People carried their paperback books on them all the time and shared titles with pride. I was rarely without a book; my walks to and from elementary school were spent reading Nancy Drew, while keeping an eye out for rogue dips and cracks in the sidewalk.

It’s different today. Kids brag about not having read a book “in years” and tease the ones who have. Attempts to impress upon them the value or pleasures of reading draw mockery. Of course it would; people don’t miss something they never knew.

I’m sitting with my 10-year-old therapy client, a shy and anxious boy whose disdain for sports and love of reading made him the perfect target for elementary school teasing.

“I know some boys who hide their books when they bring them to school,” I said, suspecting that he did this himself.

“That’s what I do!” he exclaimed, confirming my suspicions. “I hide my reading books in my book bag so no one sees them!” Nathan seemed relieved to find out he wasn’t the only kid who hid his books. The sad part about this, however, is that because these boys were all concealing their love of reading, none of them knew the others existed.

This is a different issue from just wanting to fit in. It’s kids learning that letting people see their authentic selves can end up being a social liability. And for boys who aren't particularly athletic, the social price of being smart or loving books can be even higher, because in many communities a boy who doesn't play sports and who loves to read finds himself violating two unwritten rules about what boys are supposed to want to do.

One of my sons was reading at the 10th-grade level in fifth grade. Then he went to middle school, and being neither an athlete nor a “popular” kid, Jake chose to preserve whatever social capital he had by jettisoning anything about himself that didn’t align with the suburban middle school male ideal. That meant swapping books for video games and the like. Thankfully, Jake recovered; he’s now an extraordinary English and language arts middle school teacher whose love of literature is contagious—a lovely irony.

So what if it’s your kid who’s suppressing his genuine interests because they threaten his standing among peers? Here are some conversation starters you can use to begin a discussion with him about this:

Conversation Starters for Parents

  • Introduce the idea of social pressure. Introduce the topic of “social cultures” at home in language your young son can understand. Ask him whether it’s cool or not cool to be smart in his school. Tell him you’ve heard that some boys in middle school think it’s not cool to be smart or to like reading and try to hide it from their classmates. Ask him if he ever felt like hiding how much he knew about a topic, or how well he had studied for an exam. The purpose here isn’t to resolve the problem in that moment, but rather to embark on a dialogue with your son that can be carried through over time.
  • Use a hypothetical example that feels less personal. Consider telling him a story about a kid who was really good at chess but was embarrassed to let anyone at school know. He wouldn’t even play on the school’s chess team! Ask him if he knows of anyone in his school who has done something like that. What would he do if he was really good at chess? Would he let other kids know or keep it a secret?
  • Normalize the behavior so your son doesn't feel singled out. Some boys downplay their intelligence when they’re in front of their friends. If you think your son might be doing something like this, think about how you can introduce the topic without him becoming defensive. If you start right off by asking him if he hides how smart he is from his friends, he could feel criticized or embarrassed. But by first “normalizing” the behavior, for example, by mentioning you’ve heard that a lot of boys worry about looking too smart in front of their friends, you’ll be making it easier for him to talk about it himself.
  • Respond to denial without arguing or pressing for an admission. It’s possible your son will respond by saying that’s the stupidest thing he’s ever heard, that nobody pretends to be dumber than they are. Just respond with a casual shrug and something like, "Yeah, I know, it sounds weird, but I know that in some friend groups kids get teased for studying or reading 'too much." Then let it rest. That way, he’ll understand you’re not trying to prove you’re right or “get” him to change or agree with you. People need time to make those types of changes anyway; it’s not really a “decision” you make. All you’re doing now is introducing an idea he may never have considered: that he might be hiding something valuable about himself in order to avoid being singled out, which is how change can often begin in someone who wasn’t looking for it in the first place.

item.title: What a Social Connection Number Hides
item.description:
Loneliness

What a Social Connection Number Hides

Survey tools that share a label often ask about very different things.

Posted October 25, 2026

Key points
  • What people need from connection differs by person and place, so one program won't fit everywhere.
  • Most tools that measure social connection were built in the US; only 4.7% center on adults over 65.
  • Two tools under the same heading share on average only 9% to 20% of their content.
  • Monitoring should show which form of connection is missing, and for whom, so the right department can act.

In 2022, two large European surveys asked people the same loneliness question, in nationally representative samples from all 27 EU member states. They still produced very different prevalence rates and ranked the countries differently.

Governments now spend real money on loneliness, and they need tools that show whether a program changed what it set out to change. A loneliness figure can show the size of a problem but not what is missing in people's lives. One person lacks someone to rely on in a crisis. Another sees friends every week and still feels nobody understands them. Transport, housing, social services, and culture budgets each act on a different part of that picture.

Our latest policy brief for LONELY-EU, a Horizon Europe project, asks where the tools behind these numbers came from and what they actually ask.

What We Already Knew About Loneliness

With colleagues at the European Commission's Joint Research Centre, we tested common loneliness measures in 25,646 people across all 27 member states. Only the Three-Item UCLA Loneliness Scale produced scores that could be compared from one country to the next, and its scores track emotional states more closely than social activities.

Our previous policy brief drew the first lesson: A good questionnaire cannot give Europe a dependable picture on its own; it needs coordinated yearly data collection, quality checks, and a place in Eurostat's official statistics. Another policy brief then rated common measures green, yellow, or red on comparability across countries; whether they capture loneliness and not depression; and how fully they cover what people experience. None earned green on all three. I wrote about both on this page. Our new brief looks at the whole field.

Who the Tools Were Built For

This new policy brief draws on a systematic review Annecy Behavioral Science Lab ran with Ruhr University Bochum. We screened 9,032 articles, found 2,720 different tools, and focused on the 1,859 articles that developed a new one. Development is where the basic choices get made. A later translation can test a tool in a new country, but it cannot add questions the original authors never thought to ask. The United States accounts for 33.6% of development work, and English-speaking countries for 56%. Only 18.7% involves an EU member state. Among tools with a clear age band, 52% center on adults aged 26 to 44 and 4.7% on adults aged 65 and older. Only 10.8% mention an ethnic or racial group at all.

What the Tools Ask

Researchers often sort social connection into structure, function, and quality: how many relationships people have and how often they see others, what those relationships provide, and how good or strained they feel. We coded every question in all 2,720 tools into 73 content categories, so any two tools could be compared. Tools in the same part overlap far less than their labels suggest. Two tools that both measure function share on average 15.6% of their content, structure tools 20.1%, and quality tools 9.4%. Depression scales, a field already known for varied measures, share around 36%. Two figures with the same label can describe different experiences. The survey matters too, as mode, sampling, and question order also shape results.

Different Places Need Different Solutions

The low overlap reflects how varied social connection is. In our interviews across countries, people describe connection in specific terms, such as someone to rely on, feeling understood, trust, or safety, and which of these matters differs from person to person and place to place.

For policy, that means a program that works in one setting can miss in another. A befriending scheme may help someone who lacks contact but do little for someone surrounded by family who feels misunderstood. Governments need monitoring that shows which form of connection is missing, for whom, and where, so each problem goes to the department that can act on it. Measurement has to be built for that variety, with tools developed for the people being measured.

The same gap emerges in the newer economic language around the issue. Brain capital treats people's brain health and skills as an asset worth investing in, and counts social connection as one of the drivers. So far that driver is tracked with only a couple of broad indicators. If governments are going to invest in connection the way they invest in skills, they need to know which form of it they are buying, and for whom.

What Governments Can Do Now

A long series that keeps the same question and method is still the best evidence of change over time. The brief asks statistical offices to keep those series and to publish, next to each figure, the tool used, what it captures, and how the survey was run. For new work, it recommends pairing the Three-Item UCLA scale with a few questions on contact and on having someone to rely on. Funders can ask that new tools be developed with older adults, migrants, minorities, and people in economic precarity from the start.

Within LONELY-EU we are building the EU Social Isolation and Loneliness Index for this purpose. Three core items keep countries comparable, 10 extended items serve national monitoring, and 10 more can vary between groups such as older adults. The extended version reports each form of connection separately, so a ministry could see whether a region's gap lies in contact, in support, or in feeling understood. Like any new tool, it needs independent validation before it can carry policy weight.

If you work with these numbers, look up the tool behind the next statistic you cite in the LONELY-EU Item Explorer, which shows what each published tool asks. Then check whether those questions match what your program is trying to change.

item.title: The Next Economic Frontier
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Next Economic Frontier

What if progress became better at connecting the things that matter?

Posted October 25, 2026

Imagine that artificial intelligence delivers much of what its advocates promise: Businesses become more productive. Routine administration takes minutes instead of hours. Scientists discover promising drugs and materials faster. Energy networks become easier to manage. A small company gains analytical capabilities that once required an entire department. By familiar economic measures, there would be much to celebrate.

Now widen the picture. Are people becoming more capable of shaping their lives? Are the gains reaching those who need them? Are natural systems becoming healthier? And as machines become better at writing, analyzing, remembering, and recommending, are they strengthening human capability or encouraging us to exercise less of it? These are economic questions too. They point towards what may become the next frontier of economic progression: an architecture that becomes better at generating more of what matters, by recognizing that social, economic, ecological, and technological progress are deeply intertwined.

One economy, four connected systems

We have become accustomed to dividing reality into manageable pieces. Economic ministries deal with growth. Social ministries address health, education, and inequality. Environmental agencies focus on climate, biodiversity, and pollution. Technology policy concentrates on innovation and competitiveness. The divisions make administrative sense. Life itself is less cooperative.

Take a data centre. Economically, it represents investment and productive capacity. Technologically, it provides the computing power behind AI. Socially, its significance depends on what that power enables, which jobs it changes and who benefits. Ecologically, the same facility needs electricity, water, equipment, minerals and land. One investment moves through four systems at once. The numbers make this tangible. Current energy projections suggest that the world's data centres could consume around 950 terawatt-hours of electricity annually by 2030, almost twice their 2025 consumption. That is slightly more electricity than the whole of Japan uses today. Data centres would still represent only around 3 per cent of projected global electricity demand, so the point is not that AI will consume the world's power. What matters is the speed of expansion and the pressure concentrated demand can place on particular grids.

This is happening on a planet already under strain. The 2026 Planetary Health Check finds seven of nine planetary boundaries beyond their safe operating space. In everyday language, several of the natural systems that have provided relatively stable conditions for human societies are being pushed beyond scientifically assessed limits.

AI could help. It can balance electricity networks, improve industrial efficiency, reduce waste, accelerate materials discovery and monitor forests, oceans and agriculture. Technology can increase ecological pressure and help reduce it; widen access to opportunity and concentrate economic power; relieve people of tedious work and remove experiences through which expertise develops. The effects are connected. That is why improving one part of the system while transferring costs to another resembles moving an expense between columns of a household budget and declaring ourselves richer.

Where does the productivity go?

AI makes this question urgent because productivity gains are already appearing. A large workplace experiment found that regular users of generative AI spent about two fewer hours each week on email and reduced work outside normal hours. AI, in other words, created time.

What happens to that time?

An hour saved can become another hour of production. It can also become learning, care, creativity, better customer interaction or time returned to an employee. Higher productivity can translate into lower prices, larger profits, higher wages, greater investment in social projects or better public services. Which way it goes depends on economic systems, and the human choices which they incentivice. Which links to another asset that our economic statistics capture poorly: human agency — our capacity to understand, judge, choose and act.

AI can strengthen that capacity and encourage us to exercise it less. GPS offers a familiar analogy: Navigation has become wonderfully efficient, while it is perfectly possible to travel repeatedly through a city without developing much understanding of its geography. Apply the same principle to writing, remembering, and making decisions, and the stakes become higher. In a 2026 randomized experiment AI substantially narrowed performance differences between people with different educational backgrounds while it was available. When participants later worked without AI, the gains did not translate uniformly into independent capability. How people engaged with the technology mattered. The economic challenge is consequently more sophisticated than deciding whether humans should delegate to machines.

Making progress work harder for people and planet

This is where ProSocial AI comes in. It's not about creating machines that are friendly or altruistic but developing and deploying AI with a wider understanding of value: using technological capability to improve outcomes across people, prosperity and planet rather than optimizing one measure while ignoring effects elsewhere.

The applications can be thoroughly practical. An agricultural system can help a farmer improve yields while reducing unnecessary water and fertilizer. AI can remove paperwork from a nurse's day and return time to patients. A logistics system can reduce costs and waste. A teacher can identify where a student needs support while ensuring that the student still does the thinking required to learn.

The common thread is better alignment.

This leads towards Hybrid Intelligence, a deliberate combination of natural and artificial intelligences such that their strengths complement one another. Humans contribute lived experience, values, responsibility, social understanding and judgment. Artificial systems contribute speed, scale and the ability to process quantities of information no person could reasonably manage. Both operate within natural systems on which every economy depends.

The ultimate destination is Hybrid Flourishing—a condition in which technological progress expands the capacity of people and planet to thrive, giving every living being a fair chance to fulfill its inherent potential. It grows from the inside out through human values, choices and agency, while being nurtured from the outside in by institutions, markets and technologies that support those choices. We can't abandon growth; billions of people still need better housing, healthcare, education, infrastructure and economic security. Material progress remains indispensable. The task is to ask more of it.

=> Purpose. People. Prosperity. Planet. For two centuries, economic development has become progressively better at producing more stuff, while valuing humans and nature less. Injected in the current economic architecture, AI will accelerate that "achievement". There is an alternative: creating prosperity in ways that strengthen the people, societies and living systems from which prosperity comes.

We know how to make machines more productive. The opportunity of a lifetime is making progress more productive for life.
